newsitem.title: THAILAND: Currency volatility seen good for Asian bonds.
newsitem.headline: Currency volatility seen good for Asian bonds.

text.p: Regional currency volatility after de facto devaluations of the Thai baht and Philippine peso provides attractive opportunities for the Asian bond market, a top executive at Washington Asset Management Inc (WAMI) said on Monday.
Ismail Dalla, president of the U.S.-based firm, said the volatility would make Asian bonds more market-based and allow interest rate movements that investors can make money on.

"Having more volatility in the movement of currencies and exchange rates will make it more interesting for investors as they get paid to do that," Dalla told a conference on Asian Bonds organised by the Financial Times.
"It's hard for bond markets to be built when the bond yield is flat," he said.
Thailand on July 2 cut loose its tightly-controlled baht and allowed the currency to move under a managed float system.
The Philippines on Friday succumbed to speculative attacks on the currency and widened its band, sending the peso plunging.
The jitters spread over the region. Malaysia's strong ringgit on Monday plummeted to a 16-year low of 2.5500/10 to the dollar.
Despite some slowdown in regional economies, Dalla said he was confident about the growth outlook for the region.
The size of the emerging Asian bond market was set to reach US$1.30 trillion by the year 2005 from around $390 billion in 1995, he said.
The high growth in regional bond markets would be propelled by demand for funds to finance infrastructure and privatisations.
He forecast that East Asian economies would need to invest between $1.2-$1.5 trillion over the next decade or an equivalent of seven percent of their gross domestic product (GDP).

Other factors driving bond market growth in Asia would include shifting patterns of corporate finance towards debt capital, equity markets reaching saturation, and growing institutional investor base.
Bank of International Settlement requirements that have constrained the ability of the banking sector to provide long-term finance would also benefit the bond market in Asia, he said.

According to World Bank and Washington Asset Management Inc estimates at end-1995, the size of South Korea's bond market was $190.0 billion, China's was $45.4 billion, Singapore's $46.3 billion, Malaysia's $41.6 billion, Hong Kong's $14.6 billion, the Philippines' $27.0 billion, Thailand's $16.8 billion, and Indonesia's $8.7 billion.
